listen_text: Section. Introduction. The number of truth values of a matrix need not be finite. An obvious choice for a set of infinitely many truth values is the set of rational numbers between zero and one , V subscript infinity equals the intersection of the closed interval from zero to one with the rational numbers , that is, Displayed expression. V subscript infinity equals the set of fractions n divided by m such that n and m are natural numbers and n is less than or equal to m. When considering this infinite truth value set, it is often useful to also consider the subsets V subscript m, which the source writes as the set of n divided by the quantity m minus one, such that n is a natural number and n is less than or equal to m. For instance, V subscript five is the set with five evenly spaced truth values: V subscript five equals the set containing zero, one quarter, one half, three quarters, and one. End of displayed value sets. End displayed expression. In logics based on these truth value sets, usually only one is designated, that is, the designated value set V plus is the singleton set containing one . In other words, we let one play the role of (absolute) truth, zero as absolute falsity, but formulas may take any intermediate value in V . Source anomaly note. Source value-set caveat. The displayed bound n less than or equal to m would include an extra value above one in V subscript m. The stated five-value example instead corresponds to n at most m minus one, with m at least two. The rational fraction description also needs a nonzero denominator. The original formulas are retained, and subsequent finite-valued definitions are read with this discrepancy visible. Original source remains available in Source view. End note. One can also consider the set V subscript the closed interval from zero to one equals that closed interval of all real numbers between zero and one , or other infinite subsets of the closed interval from zero to one , however. Logics with this truth value set are often called fuzzy. End section.

listen_text: Section. Łukasiewicz logic. Editorial note. This is a short “stub” of a section on infinite-valued Łukasiewicz logic. End editorial note. Definition. Infinite-valued Łukasiewicz logic L subscript infinity is defined using the matrix: List. Next item. The standard propositional language L subscript zero with negation , conjunction , disjunction , conditional . Next item. The set of truth values V subscript infinity . Next item. one is the only designated value, that is, the designated value set V plus is the singleton set containing one . Next item. Truth functions are given by the following functions: Displayed expression. Lukasiewicz truth functions. Negation of x has value one minus x. Conjunction of x and y has the minimum of x and y as its value. Disjunction has their maximum as its value. The conditional with antecedent value x and consequent value y has value the minimum of one and the quantity one minus the difference x minus y. Equivalently, its value is one if x is less than or equal to y, and one minus the difference x minus y otherwise. End of truth function definitions. End displayed expression. End list. m valued Łukasiewicz logic is defined the same, except V equals V subscript m . End definition. Proposition. The logic three valued Lukasiewicz logic defined by the earlier three valued Lukasiewicz matrix definition is the same as three valued Lukasiewicz logic defined by the infinite and finite valued Lukasiewicz matrix definition . End proposition. Proof. Columns are input and output, in that order. Row one, input one : output zero . Row two, input one half : output one half . Row three, input zero : output one . End of truth table. Truth table for the three valued Lukasiewicz conditional truth function . Rows give the first argument; columns give the second argument. Column values, in source order: one , one half , zero . Row one, input one : outputs in that column order: one , one half , zero . Row two, input one half : outputs in that column order: one , one , one half . Row three, input zero : outputs in that column order: one , one , one . End of truth table. End proof. Proposition. If Gamma entails B in infinite valued Lukasiewicz logic then Gamma entails B in m valued Lukasiewicz logic for all m greater than or equal to two . End proposition. Proof. Exercise. End proof. Exercise. Prove the proposition on restricting infinite Lukasiewicz consequence to finitely many values . End exercise. This exercise remains unsolved. In fact, the converse holds as well. Like three valued Goedel logic , infinite valued Goedel logic has all intuitionistically valid formulas as tautologies, and the same examples of non-tautologies are non-tautologies of infinite valued Goedel logic : Displayed expression. Six formulas, read across each source row from left to right. Row one, left: p or not p. Row one, right: if the conditional if p then q holds, then not p or q. Row two, left: if not not p then p. Row two, right: if it is not the case that both not p and not q, then p or q. Row three, left: if the conditional from if p then q to p holds, then p. Row three, right: if it is not the case that if p then q, then both p and not q. End of six formulas. End displayed expression. The example of an intuitionistically invalid formula that is nevertheless a tautology of three valued Goedel logic , the disjunction of if p then q with if q then p , is also a tautology in infinite valued Goedel logic . In fact, infinite valued Goedel logic can be characterized as intuitionistic logic to which the schema the disjunction of if A then B with if B then A is added. This was shown by Michael Dummett, and so infinite valued Goedel logic is often referred to as Goedel—Dummett logic L C . Exercise. Show that the disjunction of if p then q with if q then p is a tautology of infinite valued Goedel logic . End exercise. This exercise remains unsolved. Exercise. Show that the disjunction of the three conditionals: if p then q; if q then r; and if r then s , which is a tautology of three valued Goedel logic , is not a tautology of infinite valued Goedel logic . End exercise. This exercise remains unsolved. End section. End chapter.
